claim: TRIM28 potently suppresses HIV-1 expression by utilizing both SUMO E3 ligase activity and epigenetic adaptor function.
source: Here, we found that TRIM28 potently suppresses HIV-1 expression by utilizing both SUMO E3 ligase activity and epigenetic adaptor function.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript including siRNA screening, ChIP assays, and SUMOylation assays.

claim: CDK9 is significantly SUMOylated by TRIM28 with SUMO4.
source: Through global site-specific SUMO-MS study and serial SUMOylation assays, we identified that P-TEFb catalytic subunit CDK9 is significantly SUMOylated by TRIM28 with SUMO4.
evidence: This claim is supported by global site-specific SUMO-MS data, in vitro SUMOylation assays, and co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figures 3-5.

claim: The Lys44, Lys56 and Lys68 residues on CDK9 are SUMOylated by TRIM28.
source: The Lys44, Lys56 and Lys68 residues on CDK9 are SUMOylated by TRIM28, which inhibits CDK9 kinase activity or prevents P-TEFb assembly by directly blocking the interaction between CDK9 and Cyclin T1, subsequently inhibits viral transcription and contributes to HIV-1 latency.
evidence: This is supported by reversing mutation experiments, target-specific SUMO-MS, and functional assays shown in Figure 9.

claim: SUMOylation of CDK9 by TRIM28 inhibits CDK9 kinase activity.
source: The Lys44, Lys56 and Lys68 residues on CDK9 are SUMOylated by TRIM28, which inhibits CDK9 kinase activity or prevents P-TEFb assembly by directly blocking the interaction between CDK9 and Cyclin T1, subsequently inhibits viral transcription and contributes to HIV-1 latency.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro CDK9 kinase assays showing decreased activity when CDK9 is SUMOylated (Figure 8F).

claim: SUMOylation of CDK9 prevents P-TEFb assembly by blocking the interaction between CDK9 and Cyclin T1.
source: The Lys44, Lys56 and Lys68 residues on CDK9 are SUMOylated by TRIM28, which inhibits CDK9 kinase activity or prevents P-TEFb assembly by directly blocking the interaction between CDK9 and Cyclin T1, subsequently inhibits viral transcription and contributes to HIV-1 latency.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing that Cyclin T1 only binds to wild-type CDK9, not SUMOylated CDK9 (Figure 8E).

claim: The persistence of HIV-1 in latent reservoirs is the major obstacle to achieve a cure despite suppressive cART.
source: Despite the suppressive combined antiretroviral therapy (cART), the persistence of HIV-1 in the latent reservoirs is the major obstacle to achieve a cure (Chun et al., 1997; Finzi et al., 1997; Wong et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: It needs almost 73.4 years of cART to completely eradicate the HIV-1 reservoir due to its long half-life in resting CD4+ T cells.
source: To completely eradicate the reservoir, it needs almost 73.4 years of cART due to its long half-life in resting CD4+ T cells (Siliciano et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Siliciano et al., 2003.

claim: Only 1/106 resting CD4+ T cells contain inducible replication-competent proviruses.
source: Although over 200/106 resting CD4+ T cells contain proviruses, only 1/106 resting CD4+ T cells (or 1/200 of them) contain inducible replication-competent proviruses and 40/106 resting CD4+ T cells contain intact non-inducible proviruses (Eriksson et al., 2013; Ho et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eriksson et al., 2013 and Ho et al., 2013.

claim: Most HIV-1 proviruses are defective.
source: Most of the proviruses are defective, some of which can be induced to produce functional viral proteins and exposed to immunosurveillance (Ho et al., 2013; Pollack et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ho et al., 2013 and Pollack et al., 2017.

claim: Most HIV-1 integration sites locate in the intron of actively transcribed genes.
source: Most of the integration sites locate in the intron of actively transcribed genes (Schröder et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schröder et al., 2002.

claim: Integration hotspots were found in latently infected clonally expanded CD4+ T cells in HIV-1 patients on cART.
source: Some integration hotspots were found in latently infected clonally expanded CD4+ T cells in HIV-1 patients on cART (Cohn et al., 2015; Maldarelli et al., 2014; Wagner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cohn et al., 2015; Maldarelli et al., 2014; and Wagner et al., 2014.

claim: Epigenetic regulations contribute to the establishment and maintenance of HIV-1 latency.
source: Epigenetic regulations contribute to the establishment and maintenance of HIV-1 latency.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on histone deacetylases and methyltransferases in the following sentences.

claim: HDAC1 and HDAC2 are responsible for writing repressive marks on HIV-1 LTR.
source: Both histone deacetylases including HDAC1 and HDAC2, and histone methyltransferases including G9a, Suv39H1, GLP, EZH2 and SMYD2, have been found to be responsible for ''writing' repressive marks on HIV-1 long terminal repeat (LTR) (Boehm et al., 2017; Ding et al., 2013; du Chéné et al., 2007; Friedman et al., 2011; Imai et al., 2010; Marban et al., 2007; Ruelas and Greene, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including Boehm et al., 2017; Ding et al., 2013; du Chéné et al., 2007; Friedman et al., 2011; Imai et al., 2010; Marban et al., 2007; Ruelas and Greene, 2013.

claim: Histone methyltransferases including G9a, Suv39H1, GLP, EZH2 and SMYD2 are responsible for writing repressive marks on HIV-1 LTR.
source: Both histone deacetylases including HDAC1 and HDAC2, and histone methyltransferases including G9a, Suv39H1, GLP, EZH2 and SMYD2, have been found to be responsible for ''writing' repressive marks on HIV-1 long terminal repeat (LTR) (Boehm et al., 2017; Ding et al., 2013; du Chéné et al., 2007; Friedman et al., 2011; Imai et al., 2010; Marban et al., 2007; Ruelas and Greene, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including Boehm et al., 2017; Ding et al., 2013; du Chéné et al., 2007; Friedman et al., 2011; Imai et al., 2010; Marban et al., 2007; Ruelas and Greene, 2013.

claim: HP1γ and L3MBTL1 maintain suppressive epigenetic marks on HIV-1 LTR.
source: Suppressive epigenetic marks are further maintained by 'reader' proteins HP1γ and L3MBTL1 (Boehm et al., 2017; du Chéné et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boehm et al., 2017 and du Chéné et al., 2007.

claim: Multiple miRNAs including miR-28, miR-125b, miR-150, miR-223 and miR-382 target viral RNAs and viral proteins to mediate transcriptional or posttranscriptional regulations of HIV-1 latency.
source: In addition, multiple miRNAs including miR-28, miR-125b, miR-150, miR-223 and miR-382, and lncRNAs including NEAT1 and NRON, were also found to target viral RNAs and viral proteins to mediate transcriptional or posttranscriptional regulations of HIV-1 latency (Huang et al., 2007; Li et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2007; Li et al., 2016; and Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: LncRNAs including NEAT1 and NRON target viral RNAs and viral proteins to mediate transcriptional or posttranscriptional regulations of HIV-1 latency.
source: In addition, multiple miRNAs including miR-28, miR-125b, miR-150, miR-223 and miR-382, and lncRNAs including NEAT1 and NRON, were also found to target viral RNAs and viral proteins to mediate transcriptional or posttranscriptional regulations of HIV-1 latency (Huang et al., 2007; Li et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2007; Li et al., 2016; and Zhang et al., 2013.

claim: HIV-1 latency depends upon transcriptional control.
source: Apart from the above epigenetic mechanisms of HIV-1 latency, another barrier to successfully reactivate latent HIV-1 depends upon transcriptional control (Mbonye and Karn, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mbonye and Karn, 2014.

claim: HIV-1 latency is contributed by insufficiency of transcription factors including NF-κB, Sp1, AP-1, NFAT and TFIIH.
source: In transcription initiation level, HIV-1 latency is contributed by both the insufficiency of transcription factors including NF-κB, Sp1, AP-1, NFAT and TFIIH, and the accumulation of transcription suppressors including LSF, YY1 and CTIP2 (Mbonye and Karn, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mbonye and Karn, 2017.

claim: HIV-1 latency is contributed by accumulation of transcription suppressors including LSF, YY1 and CTIP2.
source: In transcription initiation level, HIV-1 latency is contributed by both the insufficiency of transcription factors including NF-κB, Sp1, AP-1, NFAT and TFIIH, and the accumulation of transcription suppressors including LSF, YY1 and CTIP2 (Mbonye and Karn, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mbonye and Karn, 2017.

claim: The absence of HIV-1 Tat and the presence of negative elongation factors NELF and DSIF facilitate promoter-proximal pausing of RNAP II on HIV-1 LTR.
source: For the escaped RNA Polymerase II (RNAP II) which passed through initiation, the absence of HIV-1 Tat and the presence of negative elongation factors NELF and DSIF facilitate promoter-proximal pausing of RNAP II on HIV-1 LTR (Ping and Rana, 2001; Razooky et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ping and Rana, 2001 and Razooky et al., 2015.

claim: RNAP II must be extensively phosphorylated at Ser2 residues by P-TEFb to escape from promoter-proximal pausing and turn to transcriptional elongation.
source: To further escape from promoter-proximal pausing and turn to transcriptional elongation, RNAP II must be extensively phosphorylated at Ser2 residues by positive transcription elongation factor b (P-TEFb), which consists of cyclin-dependent kinase 9 (CDK9) and Cyclin T1 (Ott et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ott et al., 2011.

claim: P-TEFb consists of CDK9 and Cyclin T1.
source: To further escape from promoter-proximal pausing and turn to transcriptional elongation, RNAP II must be extensively phosphorylated at Ser2 residues by positive transcription elongation factor b (P-TEFb), which consists of cyclin-dependent kinase 9 (CDK9) and Cyclin T1 (Ott et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ott et al., 2011.

claim: The expression of Cyclin T1 is downregulated in latently infected cells.
source: However, the expression of Cyclin T1 is downregulated in latently infected cells (Budhiraja et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Budhiraja et al., 2013.

claim: CDK9 is inactive in latently infected cells because of dephosphorylation of its T-loop at Thr186.
source: CDK9 is also inactive because of the dephosphorylation of its T-loop at Thr186 and sequestered in the 7SK small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (snRNP) complex by HEXIM1 or HEXIM2 (Budhiraja et al., 2013; Nguyen et al., 2001; Yang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Budhiraja et al., 2013; Nguyen et al., 2001; and Yang et al., 2001.

claim: CDK9 is sequestered in the 7SK snRNP complex by HEXIM1 or HEXIM2 in latently infected cells.
source: CDK9 is also inactive because of the dephosphorylation of its T-loop at Thr186 and sequestered in the 7SK small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (snRNP) complex by HEXIM1 or HEXIM2 (Budhiraja et al., 2013; Nguyen et al., 2001; Yang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Budhiraja et al., 2013; Nguyen et al., 2001; and Yang et al., 2001.

claim: CDK9 is acetylated at Lys44 by p300 to fully perform its kinase activity.
source: Another two studies indicate that CDK9 is acetylated at Lys44 by p300 to fully perform its kinase activity (Cho et al., 2010; Fu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cho et al., 2010 and Fu et al., 2007.

claim: Acetylation of CDK9 at Lys48 by GCN5 negatively regulates CDK9 activity.
source: Acetylation of Lys48 by GCN5 negatively regulates CDK9 activity (Sabò et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sabò et al., 2008.

claim: Knockdown of TRIM28 significantly upregulated HIV-1 promoter activity in TZM-bl cells.
source: We found that many proteins restricted the activity of HIV-1 promoter based on the expression level of luciferase upon knockdown each target (Figure 1A). The top hit proteins included HP1α, GLP, SUZ12 and CYLD, which have been identified to inhibit HIV-1 transcription (Ding et al., 2013; Khan et al., 2018; Manganaro et al., 2014). Intriguingly, we found that knockdown of two less-defined SUMOylation pathway genes TRIM28 and SUMO4 significantly upregulated HIV-1 promoter activity (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from siRNA library screening shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Knockdown of SUMO4 significantly upregulated HIV-1 promoter activity in TZM-bl cells.
source: Intriguingly, we found that knockdown of two less-defined SUMOylation pathway genes TRIM28 and SUMO4 significantly upregulated HIV-1 promoter activity (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from siRNA library screening shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Overexpression of TRIM28 inhibited the basal level of HIV-1 promoter activity in a dose-dependent manner.
source: The overexpression of TRIM28 inhibited the basal level of HIV-1 promoter activity and rescued HIV-1 repression in dose-dependent manner (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TRIM28 is ubiquitously overexpressed in multiple cell lines and primary cells.
source: We measured the expression of TRIM28 in different cells and found that TRIM28 is ubiquitously overexpressed in multiple cell lines and primary cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: TRIM28 was highly expressed in unstimulated primary CD4+ T cells and down regulated upon activation by PHA.
source: We found that TRIM28 was highly expressed in unstimulated primary CD4+ T cells and down regulated upon activation by PHA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The expression of TRIM28 was upregulated when activated CD4+ T cells returned to resting status.
source: The expression of TRIM28 was upregulated again when the activated CD4+ T cells returned to resting status (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Depletion of TRIM28 upregulated HIV-1 expression in J-Lat 10.6 cells.
source: To test whether TRIM28 contributes to HIV-1 latency, we knocked down TRIM28 in HIV-1 latency cell line J-Lat 10.6 and found that the depletion of TRIM28 upregulated HIV-1 expression (Figure 1B–C) (Jordan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B–C.

claim: HIV-1 reactivation by TRIM28 depletion was enhanced when combined with HDAC inhibitor SAHA or BET inhibitor JQ-1.
source: Besides, HIV-1 reactivation was enhanced much higher when supplemented with histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid (SAHA, vorinostat) or Bromodomain and Extra-Terminal (BET) domain inhibitor JQ-1, both of which have been widely described as LRAs (Spivak and Planelles, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B–C and citations to Spivak and Planelles, 2018.

claim: TRIM28 was significantly enriched on HIV-1 LTR compared to the regions of host-provirus junction and viral coding region.
source: We found that TRIM28 was significantly enriched on HIV-1 LTR compared to the regions of host-provirus junction and viral coding region (Figure 1D–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1D–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 3F.

claim: Depletion of TRIM28 resulted in significant decrease of H3K9me2 and H3K9me3 on HIV-1 LTR.
source: We observed significant decrease of H3K9me2 and H3K9me3, as well as significant increase of H3K4me3 and H3K9Ac after knocking down TRIM28 (Figure 1F–I, Figure 1—figure supplement 3H–J).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1F–I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3H–J.

claim: Depletion of TRIM28 resulted in significant increase of H3K4me3 and H3K9Ac on HIV-1 LTR.
source: We observed significant decrease of H3K9me2 and H3K9me3, as well as significant increase of H3K4me3 and H3K9Ac after knocking down TRIM28 (Figure 1F–I, Figure 1—figure supplement 3H–J).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1F–I and Figure 1—figure supplement 3H–J.

claim: Depletion of TRIM28 induced slight H3K27me3 downregulation on HIV-1 LTR.
source: The depletion of TRIM28 also induced slight H3K27me3 downregulation (Figure 1J, Figure 1—figure supplement 3K).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 3K.

claim: The RING domain of TRIM28 functions as an intermolecular SUMO E3 ligase.
source: The RING of TRIM28 functions as an intermolecular SUMO E3 ligase, while PHD is important for the intramolecular SUMO E3 ligase activity (Ivanov et al., 2007; Liang et al., 2011; Neo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ivanov et al., 2007; Liang et al., 2011; and Neo et al., 2015.

claim: The PHD domain of TRIM28 is important for intramolecular SUMO E3 ligase activity.
source: The RING of TRIM28 functions as an intermolecular SUMO E3 ligase, while PHD is important for the intramolecular SUMO E3 ligase activity (Ivanov et al., 2007; Liang et al., 2011; Neo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ivanov et al., 2007; Liang et al., 2011; and Neo et al., 2015.

claim: The TRIM28 mutant without RING or RBCC domains totally aborted HIV-1 re-suppression.
source: Nevertheless, the mutant without RING or RBCC domains totally aborted the re-suppression, which might be due to the loss of the Krüppel-associated box domain zinc fingers (KRAB-ZNFs) binding ability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The TRIM28 mutant containing only RBCC domain still resumed HIV-1 suppression.
source: We tested a mutant containing only RBCC. Interestingly, it still resumed the suppression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Wild-type TRIM28 was able to rescue suppressive epigenetic marks H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 on HIV-1 promoter.
source: The results showed that the wild-type TRIM28 was able to rescue the suppressive epigenetic marks H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 and suppress the active epigenetic mark H3K9Acetyl, however, the mutant without RING or PHD domain was only able to rescue partial of the suppressive marks (Figure 2C–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The TRIM28 mutant without RING or PHD domain was only able to rescue partial suppressive epigenetic marks.
source: The results showed that the wild-type TRIM28 was able to rescue the suppressive epigenetic marks H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 and suppress the active epigenetic mark H3K9Acetyl, however, the mutant without RING or PHD domain was only able to rescue partial of the suppressive marks (Figure 2C–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: 1,329 SUMOylated proteins were identified at significance threshold below 10−7 by global site-specific SUMO-MS.
source: Finally, we identified 1,329 SUMOyalted proteins at significance threshold below 10−7 (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data listed in Supplementary file 4.

claim: Many SUMOylated candidates including JUN, JUNB, JUND, mTOR, STAT3, Cyclin T1 and CDK9 are pivotal for HIV-1 expression.
source: Interestingly, we found that many candidates were pivotal for HIV-1 expression, such as JUN, JUNB, JUND, mTOR, STAT3, Cyclin T1 (CCNT1) and CDK9 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by STRING network analysis shown in Figure 3C and established knowledge about these factors in HIV-1 biology.

claim: Several transcription factors including NFKB1A, RelA, CCNT1, CDK9, SKIP, MEN1 and JUN were SUMOylated when co-overexpressed with SUMO system proteins.
source: Then, we co-overexpressed SUMO system proteins (SUMO1, SUMO2, SUMO4, UBC9 and TRIM28) with 10 transcription factor candidates, respectively. Several transcription factors were SUMOylated, such as NFKB1A, RelA, CCNT1, CDK9, SKIP, MEN1 and JUN, which verified the reliability of our global site-specific SUMO-MS (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The SUMOylation signals were much more significant for CDK9 compared to other transcription factors.
source: Nevertheless, the SUMOylation signals were much more significant for CDK9, which merited being further studied.
evidence: This is based on comparison of SUMOylation signals shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Depletion of SUMO4 upregulated HIV-1 promoter activity more significantly than depletion of other SUMO paralogs.
source: It is worthy to note that the depletion of SUMO4 was able to upregulate the HIV-1 promoter activity more significantly than the depletion of the other SUMO paralogs in our siRNA library screening (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by siRNA screening data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Knockdown or knockout of SUMO4 was able to reactivate latent pseudotyped HIV-1 in J-Lat 10.6 cells.
source: The knockdown or knockout of SUMO4 was able to reactivate latent pseudotyped HIV-1 in J-Lat 10.6 as well (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: SUMO4 is ubiquitously overexpressed in multiple cell lines and primary CD4+ T cells.
source: SUMO4 is also ubiquitously overexpressed in multiple cell lines and primary CD4+ T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The expression of SUMO4 was downregulated after PHA stimulation in primary CD4+ T cells.
source: After PHA stimulation in primary CD4+ T cells, the expression of SUMO4 was downregulated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The expression of SUMO4 returned to basal level when activated primary CD4+ T cells re-entered resting status.
source: The expression SUMO4 returned to basal level when activated primary CD4+ T cells re-entered to resting status (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: More than half of TRIM28 was lost from HIV-1 LTR upon SUMO4 knockdown.
source: We found that more than half of TRIM28 was lost from HIV-1 LTR upon SUMO4 knockdown, which indicated that the enrichment of TRIM28 on HIV-1 LTR may be partially SUMOylation-dependent apart from the Krüppel-associated box domain zinc fingers (KRAB-ZNFs)–dependent binding (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–H).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–H.

claim: H3K9me, H3K9me2 and H3K9me3 were significantly decreased on HIV-1 LTR in the absence of SUMO4.
source: We also found that H3K9me, H3K9me2 and H3K9me3 were significantly decreased on HIV-1 LTR in the absence of SUMO4, as well as the H3K9 methylation 'writer' SETDB1 and 'reader' HP1α (Figure 4E–G, Figure 4K–L).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4E–G and Figure 4K–L.

claim: SETDB1 and HP1α were decreased on HIV-1 LTR in the absence of SUMO4.
source: We also found that H3K9me, H3K9me2 and H3K9me3 were significantly decreased on HIV-1 LTR in the absence of SUMO4, as well as the H3K9 methylation 'writer' SETDB1 and 'reader' HP1α (Figure 4E–G, Figure 4K–L).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4E–G and Figure 4K–L.

claim: Significant upregulation of H3K9acetyl and H3K4me3 was observed upon SUMO4 knockdown.
source: Moreover, we observed significant upregulation of H3K9acetyl and H3K4me3 and downregulation of HDAC1, which was consistent with previous reports that TRIM28 recruited SETDB1, HP1α and HDAC1 in a SUMOylation-dependent manner (Figure 4H–I, Figure 4M) (Iyengar and Farnham, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4H–I and Figure 4M, and citation to Iyengar and Farnham, 2011.

claim: HDAC1 was downregulated on HIV-1 LTR upon SUMO4 knockdown.
source: Moreover, we observed significant upregulation of H3K9acetyl and H3K4me3 and downregulation of HDAC1, which was consistent with previous reports that TRIM28 recruited SETDB1, HP1α and HDAC1 in a SUMOylation-dependent manner (Figure 4H–I, Figure 4M) (Iyengar and Farnham, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4H–I and Figure 4M, and citation to Iyengar and Farnham, 2011.

claim: H3K27me3 was decreased on HIV-1 LTR upon SUMO4 knockdown.
source: Besides, we found that the H3K27me3 was also decreased on HIV-1 LTR upon SUMO4 knockdown (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: CDK9 was mainly SUMOylated with SUMO1 and SUMO4.
source: We co-overexpressed CDK9 with SUMO1, SUMO2 and SUMO4, respectively. We found that CDK9 was mainly SUMOylated with SUMO1 and SUMO4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I.

claim: The SUMO4-CDK9 amount was much more abundant than the SUMO1-CDK9 amount.
source: The SUMO4-CDK9 amount was much more abundant than the SUMO1-CDK9 amount.
evidence: This is based on comparison of SUMOylation signals in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I.

claim: TRIM28 utilized more SUMO4 compared with SUMO1 and SUMO2.
source: Besides, SUMO E3 ligase TRIM28 utilized more SUMO4 compared with SUMO1 and SUMO2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1J.

claim: TRIM28-mediated SUMOylation was UBC9-dependent.
source: However, the SUMOyaltion did not increase if we only co-overexpressed CDK9 with TRIM28 but without SUMO E2 UBC9, which indicated that TRIM28-mediated SUMOylation was UBC9-dependent (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The SUMO-CDK9 amount increased dose-dependently when TRIM28 increased gradually.
source: The SUMO-CDK9 amount was increased dose-dependently when the TRIM28 increased gradually (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: SUMO4 was conjugated to CDK9 only when SUMO4, E1 SAE1/UBA2, E2 UBC9 and TRIM28 were supplied together in vitro.
source: Only when SUMO4, E1 SAE1/UBA2, E2 UBC9 and TRIM28 were supplied into the SUMO conjugation reaction buffer together, was SUMO4 conjugated to CDK9 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro SUMOylation assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: SUMOylated CDK9 decreased after knocking down TRIM28 in HeLa cells.
source: After knocking down TRIM28 in HeLa cells, the SUMOylated CDK9 decreased (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: SENP3 prevented TRIM28-mediated CDK9 SUMOylation.
source: We then co-overexpressed SENP3 with TRIM28 and found that SENP3 prevented TRIM28-mediated CDK9 SUMOylation (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A small portion of endogenous CDK9 was SUMOylated by SUMO4 in primary CD4+ T cells.
source: We also immunoblotted the endogenous CDK9 in primary CD4+ T cells and found that a small portion of CDK9 was SUMOylated by SUMO4 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: SUMO4-SUMOylated endogenous CDK9 increased significantly after overexpression of SUMO4, UBC9 and TRIM28 in primary CD4+ T cells.
source: The SUMO4-SUMOylated endogenous CDK9 increased significantly after the overexpression of SUMOylation components including SUMO4, UBC9 and TRIM28 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: TRIM28 existed in many small clusters and large bodies in the nucleus and co-localized with dotted SUMO4.
source: We found that TRIM28 existed in many small clusters and large bodies in the nucleus and co-localized with dotted SUMO4 (Figure 6A, first panel).
evidence: This is supported by cSTORM imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: SUMO4 proteins were enriched by TRIM28 and shaped big spots.
source: From amplified view and 3D-cSTORM, we found that SUMO4 proteins were enriched by TRIM28 and shaped big spots (Figure 6A, second and third panels; Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by cSTORM imaging data shown in Figure 6A and Video 1.

claim: CDK9 co-localized with TRIM28 in the nucleus.
source: Although CDK9 existed in dispersed dots all within the nucleus, we still found that CDK9 co-localized with TRIM28 (Figure 6B, first panel).
evidence: This is supported by cSTORM imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: CDK9 proteins were enriched by and surrounded TRIM28 bodies.
source: Similarly to SUMO4, CDK9 proteins were enriched by and surrounded TRIM28 bodies (Figure 6B, second and third panels; Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by cSTORM imaging data shown in Figure 6B and Video 2.

claim: Nearly 80% of TRIM28 spots or complexes were co-localized with 94% of SUMO4 spots.
source: Finally, we found that nearly 80% of TRIM28 spots or complexes were co-localized with 94% of SUMO4 spots (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative co-localization analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: 88% of TRIM28 spots or complexes were co-localized with 76% of CDK9 spots.
source: Similarly, 88% of TRIM28 spots or complexes were co-localized with 76% of CDK9 spots (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative co-localization analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: CDK9 bound to TRIM28 even in the presence of RNase.
source: Through co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) assay, we found that CDK9 bound to TRIM28, even in the presence of RNase (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The depletion of RING domain aborted the binding of CDK9 to TRIM28.
source: The depletion of RING aborted the binding of CDK9 as well as the SUMOylation of CDK9 (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP and SUMOylation assay data shown in Figure 7A–B.

claim: The depletion of RING domain aborted the SUMOylation of CDK9.
source: The depletion of RING aborted the binding of CDK9 as well as the SUMOylation of CDK9 (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP and SUMOylation assay data shown in Figure 7A–B.

claim: Exogenously expressed TRIM28 co-localized with CDK9 with Pearson's coefficient of 0.7336 and thresholded Mander's coefficient of 0.5846.
source: Exogenously expressed TRIM28 also co-localized with CDK9 with Pearson's coefficient of 0.7336 and thresholded Mander's coefficient of 0.5846, which indicated a highly co-localization.
evidence: This is supported by SIM imaging and quantitative co-localization analysis shown in Figure 7C–D.

claim: The TRIM28 mutant with RING domain deletion was not capable of co-localizing with CDK9.
source: However, the mutant of RING domain deletion was not capable (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: This is supported by SIM imaging and quantitative co-localization analysis shown in Figure 7C–D.

claim: All TRIM28 mutants were SUMOylated and enriched UBC9.
source: We also inspected the SUMOylation status of each TRIM28 mutants and found that all the mutants was SUMOylated, which coincided with previous reports that both the RING and PHD had the E3 ligase activity and enriched UBC9 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) (Ivanov et al., 2007; Liang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and citations to Ivanov et al., 2007 and Liang et al., 2011.

claim: The accessible region indicated by transposable tag density increased on HIV-1 LTR when TRIM28 was knocked out from J-lat 10.6 cell lines.
source: We found that the accessible region indicated by transposable tag density increased on HIV-1 LTR when TRIM28 was knocked out from J-lat 10.6 cell lines, as well as when TRIM28 was knocked down in TZM-bl cell lines, which indicated significantly enhanced promoter activity (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-Seq data shown in Figure 8A–B.

claim: The accessible region indicated by transposable tag density increased on HIV-1 LTR when TRIM28 was knocked down in TZM-bl cell lines.
source: We found that the accessible region indicated by transposable tag density increased on HIV-1 LTR when TRIM28 was knocked out from J-lat 10.6 cell lines, as well as when TRIM28 was knocked down in TZM-bl cell lines, which indicated significantly enhanced promoter activity (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-Seq data shown in Figure 8A–B.

claim: Significant enrichment of CDK9 on HIV-1 LTR was observed upon knockdown of TRIM28.
source: Alternatively, we also observed significant enrichment of CDK9 and Ser2 super-phosphorylated RNAP II on HIV-1 LTR upon the knockdown of either TRIM28 or SUMO4, which was in agreement with the results that the depletion of TRIM28 or SUMO4 reactivated HIV-1 expression (Figure 8C–D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 8C–D.

claim: Significant enrichment of Ser2 super-phosphorylated RNAP II on HIV-1 LTR was observed upon knockdown of TRIM28.
source: Alternatively, we also observed significant enrichment of CDK9 and Ser2 super-phosphorylated RNAP II on HIV-1 LTR upon the knockdown of either TRIM28 or SUMO4, which was in agreement with the results that the depletion of TRIM28 or SUMO4 reactivated HIV-1 expression (Figure 8C–D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 8C–D.

claim: Significant enrichment of CDK9 on HIV-1 LTR was observed upon knockdown of SUMO4.
source: Alternatively, we also observed significant enrichment of CDK9 and Ser2 super-phosphorylated RNAP II on HIV-1 LTR upon the knockdown of either TRIM28 or SUMO4, which was in agreement with the results that the depletion of TRIM28 or SUMO4 reactivated HIV-1 expression (Figure 8C–D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 8C–D.

claim: Significant enrichment of Ser2 super-phosphorylated RNAP II on HIV-1 LTR was observed upon knockdown of SUMO4.
source: Alternatively, we also observed significant enrichment of CDK9 and Ser2 super-phosphorylated RNAP II on HIV-1 LTR upon the knockdown of either TRIM28 or SUMO4, which was in agreement with the results that the depletion of TRIM28 or SUMO4 reactivated HIV-1 expression (Figure 8C–D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 8C–D.

claim: Cyclin T1 only bound to wild-type CDK9, not SUMOylated CDK9.
source: Interestingly, through Co-IP assay, we found that Cyclin T1 only bound to wild-type CDK9 to form P-TEFb complex, not the SUMOylated CDK9 (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The kinase activity of CDK9 significantly decreased when SUMOylated by TRIM28.
source: We found that the kinase activity of CDK9 significantly decreased when SUMOylated by TRIM28.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The kinase activity of CDK9 was not influenced without the addition of TRIM28, although other SUMOylation components were added.
source: However, the kinase activity of CDK9 was not influenced without the addition of TRIM28, although the other SUMOylation components have been added (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The CDK9-K0R construct totally aborted the capability of CDK9 to be SUMOylated.
source: The construct named CDK9-K0R, which contained the mutation that all the lysines were changed to arginines, totally aborted the capability of CDK9 to be SUMOylated (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by SUMOylation assay data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Multiple SUMOylation sites exist across the whole CDK9 sequence.
source: However, the other CDK9 mutants still were able to be SUMOylated by TRIM28, which indicated that multiple SUMOylation sites might exist across the whole CDK9 sequence.
evidence: This is based on SUMOylation assay data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1B and inference from the results.

claim: Several lysines on CDK9 were significantly SUMOylated based on reversing mutation strategy.
source: Finally, we found that several lysines on CDK9 were significantly SUMOylated (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by SUMOylation assay data using reversing mutation constructs shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Multiple SUMOylation sites on CDK9 were adjacent to C-terminal autophosphorylation sites required for high-affinity binding of Tat–P-TEFb to TAR RNA.
source: Among them, multiple SUMOylation sites were adjacent to CDK9 C-terminal autophosphorylation sites which have been reported to be required for high-affinity binding of Tat–P-TEFb to TAR RNA (Baumli et al., 2008; Garber et al., 2000).
evidence: This is based on analysis of SUMOylation sites and citations to Baumli et al., 2008 and Garber et al., 2000.

claim: The SUMOylation signals of Lys44, Lys56 and Lys68 totally disappeared in the absence of endogenous TRIM28.
source: We found that the SUMOylation signals of Lys44, Lys56 and Lys68 totally disappeared in the absence of endogenous TRIM28, further supporting that these sites are specifically SUMOylated by TRIM28 (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by SUMOylation assay data with TRIM28 knockdown shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Target-specific SUMO-MS confirmed that Lys44, Lys56 and Lys68 are SUMOylated by TRIM28.
source: The target-specific SUMO-MS for directly analyzing the enriched SUMO-CDK9 also confirmed this result (Figure 9—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by target-specific SUMO-MS data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1C–E.

claim: Lys56 and Lys68 are within the interaction region of CDK9 and Cyclin T1.
source: Interestingly, other two SUMOylated sites Lys56 and Lys68 are within the interaction region of CDK9 and Cyclin T1 based on the co-crystal structure (PDB ID: 4EC8) (Baumli et al., 2012) (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis using co-crystal structure data (PDB ID: 4EC8) shown in Figure 9C and citation to Baumli et al., 2012.

claim: The depletion of TRIM28 was non-toxic to cell viability and proliferation.
source: The results showed that the depletion of TRIM28 was non-toxic to cell viability and proliferation (Figure 10—figure supplement 1, Figure 10—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity, cell viability, cell counting, and proliferation assay data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1 and Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: Stimulation with αCD3/αCD28 significantly induced the expression of HIV-1 in resting CD4+ T cells from HIV-1-infected individuals.
source: Stimulation with αCD3/αCD28 significantly induced the expression of HIV-1 based on the quantitation of intracellular HIV-1 RNAs (Figure 10A and Figure 10—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 10A and Figure 10—figure supplement 3A–B.

claim: The depletion of TRIM28 reactivated similar amount of HIV-1 RNA as SAHA in resting CD4+ T cells from HIV-1-infected individuals.
source: The depletion of TRIM28 reactivated similar amount of HIV-1 RNA as suberanilohydroxamic acid (SAHA).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: The combination of TRIM28 knockdown with SAHA resulted in more significant HIV-1 reactivation than either treatment alone.
source: After we combined the knockdown of TRIM28 with SAHA, the reactivation was more significant (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: The depletion of SUMO4 reactivated substantial productions of HIV-1 RNAs in resting CD4+ T cells from HIV-1-infected individuals.
source: The results showed that the depletion of SUMO4 reactivated substantial productions of HIV-1 RNAs which were even slightly higher than those activated by SAHA.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 4.

claim: The combination of SUMO4 knockdown and SAHA reactivated more HIV-1 RNAs than either treatment alone.
source: The combination use of SUMO4 knockdown and SAHA addition could reactivate more HIV-1 RNAs than those reactivated by them separately (Figure 10—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 4.

claim: TRIM28 depletion alone reactivated similar amount of genetically diversified HIV-1 as SAHA.
source: Although TRIM28 depletion alone reactivated similar amount of genetically diversified HIV-1 with SAHA, the combination of TRIM28 knockdown and SAHA reactivated much more genetically-diversified HIV-1 (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is supported by genetic diversity analysis shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The combination of TRIM28 knockdown and SAHA reactivated much more genetically-diversified HIV-1 than either treatment alone.
source: Although TRIM28 depletion alone reactivated similar amount of genetically diversified HIV-1 with SAHA, the combination of TRIM28 knockdown and SAHA reactivated much more genetically-diversified HIV-1 (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is supported by genetic diversity analysis shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The knockdown of TRIM28 reactivated replication-competent viruses in resting CD4+ T cells from HIV-1-infected individuals.
source: The knockdown of TRIM28 reactivated replication-competent viruses in all the three samples (Figure 10C and Figure 10—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by virus outgrowth assay data shown in Figure 10C and Figure 10—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The combination of SAHA with TRIM28 knockdown reactivated more replication-competent viral particles than either treatment alone.
source: Similarly, the combination of SAHA with TRIM28 knockdown reactivated more replication-competent viral particles.
evidence: This is supported by virus outgrowth assay data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: TRIM28 has been identified as an epigenetic adaptor recruiting HP1, SETDB1 and NuRD complex to maintain suppressive epigenetic environment.
source: Because TRIM28 was identified as an epigenetic adaptor recruiting HP1, SETDB1 and NuRD complex to maintain suppressive epigenetic environment, we then tested whether the depletion of TRIM28 would influence the epigenetic status of HIV-1 LTR (Iyengar and Farnham, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Iyengar and Farnham, 2011.

claim: TRIM28 has been found to recruit multiple suppressive epigenetic modifiers to the LTRs of endogenous retroviruses.
source: TRIM28 has been found as an epigenetic adaptor which recruits multiple suppressive epigenetic modifiers to the LTRs of endogenous retroviruses (Rowe et al., 2010; Wolf and Goff, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rowe et al., 2010 and Wolf and Goff, 2007.

claim: TRIM28 has been identified to stabilize promoter-proximal pausing of RNAP II.
source: It is also identified to stabilize promoter-proximal pausing of RNAP II with some unsolved functions (Bunch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bunch et al., 2014.

claim: TRIM28 is a SUMO E3 ligase that can mediate intramolecular SUMOylation of its bromodomain.
source: Furthermore, TRIM28 is also a SUMO E3 ligase which can mediate intramolecular SUMOylation of its bromodomain and intermolecular SUMOylation of IFN regulatory factor 7 (IRF7), resulting in the recruitment of epigenetic modifiers and the inhibition of IRF7 function, respectively (Ivanov et al., 2007; Liang et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ivanov et al., 2007 and Liang et al., 2011.

claim: TRIM28 can mediate intermolecular SUMOylation of IRF7, resulting in inhibition of IRF7 function.
source: Furthermore, TRIM28 is also a SUMO E3 ligase which can mediate intramolecular SUMOylation of its bromodomain and intermolecular SUMOylation of IFN regulatory factor 7 (IRF7), resulting in the recruitment of epigenetic modifiers and the inhibition of IRF7 function, respectively (Ivanov et al., 2007; Liang et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ivanov et al., 2007 and Liang et al., 2011.

claim: In active status, P-TEFb complex is recruited by HIV-1 Tat to the partly transcribed HIV-1 RNA TAR.
source: In active status, P-TEFb complex is recruited by HIV-1 Tat to the partly transcribed HIV-1 RNA trans-activation response element (TAR).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about HIV-1 transcription mechanisms described in the model (Figure 10D).

claim: P-TEFb catalytic subunit CDK9 super-phosphorylates the Ser2 residues of RNAP II, facilitating the processivity of RNAP II on transcribing HIV-1 RNA.
source: P-TEFb catalytic subunit CDK9 super-phosphorylates the Ser2 residues of RNAP II, facilitating the processivity of RNAP II on the transcribing HIV-1 RNA.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about P-TEFb function described in the model (Figure 10D).

claim: In latent status, TRIM28 is recruited to HIV-1 LTR and SUMOylates CDK9 in Lys44, Lys56 and Lys68.
source: In latent status, TRIM28 is recruited to HIV-1 LTR and SUMOylates CDK9 in Lys44, Lys56 and Lys68, resulting in the inhibition of CDK9 kinase activity and its disconnecting with Cyclin T1.
evidence: This is based on the experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript and summarized in the model (Figure 10D).

claim: SUMOylation of CDK9 by TRIM28 results in inhibition of CDK9 kinase activity and disconnection with Cyclin T1.
source: In latent status, TRIM28 is recruited to HIV-1 LTR and SUMOylates CDK9 in Lys44, Lys56 and Lys68, resulting in the inhibition of CDK9 kinase activity and its disconnecting with Cyclin T1.
evidence: This is based on the experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript and summarized in the model (Figure 10D).

claim: Without super-phosphorylation on Ser2, RNAP II promoter-proximal pauses at HIV-1 LTR.
source: Without the super-phosphorylation on Ser2, RNAP II promoter-proximal paused at LTR.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about RNAP II regulation and the experimental findings in this study.

claim: Latent status is maintained by both TRIM28-mediated CDK9 dysfunction and TRIM28-mediated suppressive epigenetic modification on nucleosome nuc-1.
source: Therefore, the latent status is maintained by both TRIM28-mediated CDK9 dysfunction and TRIM28-mediated suppressive epigenetic modification on nucleosome nuc-1 which lies precisely downstream of HIV-1 promoter (Verdin et al., 1993).
evidence: This is based on the experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript and citation to Verdin et al., 1993.
